821.quote_or_event: “False is friendship with the false and greedy. False is its foundation. O Moollah, no one knows where death shall strike.”
821.explanation: In a salok added after the vaars, Guru Nanak warns that a bond formed with the false and greedy rests on a false foundation, and sets it beside the unpredictability of death's blow.
821.tie_back: The Kural pictures false friendship as an anvil that looks like support but is the base for a blow; Guru Nanak likewise calls such friendship false at its very foundation.
821.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Saloks Vaaran Te Vadheek (salok 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
821._accuracy_note: Close on the false foundation of insincere friendship; the 'strike' in Gurbani is death's, not the false friend's, so the anvil image is matched only in part.

822.quote_or_event: “I thought that he was a great swan, so I associated with him. If I had known that he was only a wretched heron from birth, I would not have touched him.”
822.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the swan and heron (a bird that only looks like a swan) to describe one who passes for a true companion but is of another nature altogether.
822.tie_back: The Kural speaks of people who seem like one's own kind but are not; Guru Amar Das's heron that looked like a swan is the same kind of false likeness.
822.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 585, Raag Vadahans, Vadahans Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 1), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
822._accuracy_note: Strong on the look-alike who is not truly kin; the Kural's further point that such bonds shift with gain is not in this salok.

823.quote_or_event: “That scholar who is full of greed, arrogant pride and egotism, is known to be a fool.”
823.explanation: In Majh Ki Vaar Guru Nanak denies that learning by itself makes a person good: a scholar ruled by greed and ego is still counted a fool.
823.tie_back: The Kural warns that those hostile at heart are not made good-hearted by much study; Guru Nanak likewise says learning does not cure a corrupt heart.
823.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Majh, Majh Ki Vaar (pauri 6), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
823._accuracy_note: Shares the point that learning does not reform the heart, but the verse is about scholars in general, not learned enemies posing as friends.

824.quote_or_event: “Farid, you wear your prayer shawl on your shoulders and the robes of a Sufi; your words are sweet, but there is a dagger in your heart. Outwardly, you look bright, but your heart is dark as night.”
824.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid exposes the person whose outward look and sweet words hide a dagger within.
824.tie_back: The Kural says to fear deceivers who smile with the face while the heart is bitter; Farid's sweet words with a dagger in the heart are the same split between face and heart.
824.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1380, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 50) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
824._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match of bright face and dark heart; Farid addresses it as self-examination as well as a warning about others.

825.quote_or_event: “Whatever is in the mind, comes forth; spoken words by themselves are just wind.”
825.explanation: In a salok in Asa Ki Vaar, Guru Angad teaches that what counts is what is in the mind, while words cut off from it are only air.
825.tie_back: The Kural says the words of those not one with you in heart cannot be relied on; Guru Angad likewise calls words empty when the heart is not behind them.
825.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
825._accuracy_note: Strong on words being worthless apart from the heart; Guru Angad speaks of speech before God, not specifically of trusting an insincere friend.

826.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I have seen a person who is as shiny as washed wax. He seems very clever and very virtuous, but in reality, he is without understanding, and corrupt.”
826.explanation: In his saloks, Kabir describes seeing through a person who looks polished, clever and virtuous but is corrupt underneath.
826.tie_back: The Kural says the good words of foes posing as friends are quickly seen for what they are; Kabir likewise sees through the shiny surface to what lies beneath.
826.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 139) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
826._accuracy_note: Matches the idea of a false surface being seen through, but Kabir speaks of seeming virtue in general rather than an enemy's friendly words.

827.quote_or_event: “Everyone bows down to himself; no one bows down to another. … The sinner, like the deer hunter, bows down twice as much. But what can be achieved by bowing the head, when the heart is impure?”
827.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak observes that the hunter stalking a deer bends lowest of all, so deep bowing can serve harm, and bowing means nothing when the heart is impure.
827.tie_back: The Kural says a foe's humble speech is like the bending of a bow, which bends only to harm; Guru Nanak's sinner who bows twice as much, like the hunter, makes the same point.
827.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 1 before pauri 14), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
827._accuracy_note: Very close: both use a hunter's bending to show that outward humility can hide intent to harm.

828.quote_or_event: “The man-eaters say their prayers. Those who wield the knife wear the sacred thread around their necks. … in their hands they hold the knives - they are the butchers of the world!”
828.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak attacks oppressors of his day who perform prayers and wear religious marks while holding the knife against others.
828.tie_back: The Kural says a weapon may lie hidden in hands joined in worship; Guru Nanak likewise shows the knife held by those who make a show of prayer.
828.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 16), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
828._accuracy_note: Strong on piety masking violence; Guru Nanak's target is religious and political hypocrisy in society, not a personal enemy's feigned friendship.

829.quote_or_event: “One who offers both respectful greetings and rude refusal to his master, has gone wrong from the very beginning. O Nanak! Both of his actions are false; he obtains no place in the Court of the Lord.”
829.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Angad condemns double conduct, outward respect together with inner refusal, as false from the start.
829.tie_back: The Kural advises answering a scornful false friend with an outward smile while letting the friendship die inside; Guru Angad treats any such split between outward show and inner stance as falsehood.
829.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok 2 before pauri 21), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
829._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani shares the Kural's diagnosis of two-faced conduct but does not approve meeting pretence with pretence, which the Kural here allows as policy.

830.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur in 1704, the Mughal commanders and the allied hill chiefs offered Guru Gobind Singh safe passage, backed by an assurance sworn on the Quran and an oath by the cow. The Guru had advised staying, but under starvation the Sikhs left the fort, and they were attacked near the Sarsa river with all the oaths broken.
830.explanation: Sikh historical memory treats the broken oaths of Anandpur as the classic case of enemies offering friendship that was never meant, and Guru Gobind Singh's Zafarnama later rebuked Aurangzeb for them.
830.tie_back: The Kural says that when an enemy turns friendly one may be friendly in face but must keep friendship out of the heart; the Guru's distrust of the oaths at Anandpur shows why.
830.source: Wikipedia, 'Second siege of Anandpur' (citing Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 5, and J. S. Grewal, Guru Gobind Singh, 2019)
830._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested event checked only on Wikipedia (last resort), which cites Macauliffe and Grewal; it shows enemies' feigned friendship but not the Kural's tactic of outward friendliness.
